frontend.prompt:
Implement client-side behavior so the UI uses the server-side sorting and never performs a local re-sort of the currently-displayed page. Do not change existing filtering logic or pagination controls. Required tasks:

1) Request-level contract
- Always include a query parameter named sort with one of the two allowed enum values: "created_at_desc" or "title_asc". Do not send other values. If the user has not explicitly chosen a sort option, send sort=created_at_desc (the default) rather than omitting the parameter—this guarantees identical semantics across pages and clients.
- Preserve the chosen sort value across pagination requests (every page request must include the same sort value). When the user changes sort, switch to page=1 (or your existing first-page mechanism) and include the new sort value.

2) UI behavior
- Expose only the two allowed sort choices in the UI control: created_at_desc and title_asc (use human-friendly labels if needed). The initial control state must reflect created_at_desc unless the app explicitly shows a saved preference.
- When a sort selection changes, fetch the sorted results from the server (page 1) using the sort parameter. Do not locally reorder entries already shown on the current page; always fetch from the server and replace the page contents with the server response.

3) Error handling (422)
- If the server returns HTTP 422 for an invalid sort, surface a clear validation message to the user. Then programmatically set the client sort state to created_at_desc and immediately retry the request with sort=created_at_desc (only one automatic retry). If your app has a standard error payload format, map the server response into that format; if not, expect a JSON body containing an error code "invalid_sort" and a human message.

4) Tests / Acceptance criteria (frontend)
- Outgoing requests must always include sort with one of the allowed values; test initial load (no explicit choice) sends sort=created_at_desc.
- When user changes sort to title_asc, requests use sort=title_asc and page resets to first page.
- When paginating forward/back, requests preserve the chosen sort parameter.
- The client does not locally reorder items of the current page; verify that after changing only client-side state (without refetch), items remain unchanged until a server response replaces them.
- When server responds 422 for sort, the UI displays the validation error and then sends a request with sort=created_at_desc once.

Notes / implementation constraints
- Do not change existing server-side filtering rules or pagination parameters. If the existing API uses a different query-parameter name for pagination or error format, adapt to those conventions but keep the sort parameter name as "sort" and allowed values as specified.
- Do not invent additional sort values or client-only transforms of order; the server is authoritative for ordering.

backend.prompt:
Implement server-side validation and deterministic sorting behavior for the new sort enum and ensure sorting happens before pagination. Preserve all existing filtering behavior and existing pagination parameters. Required tasks:

1) API contract and validation
- Accept a query parameter named sort. Valid values: exactly "created_at_desc" and "title_asc". If the parameter is omitted, treat as if sort=created_at_desc (default).
- If the client supplies any other value for sort, return HTTP 422 Unprocessable Entity. The response body must convey the validation error; if your service has an existing error-format, use that. If not, return a JSON object with at least { "error": "invalid_sort", "message": "unsupported sort value" } (adapt to existing conventions if present).

2) Sorting semantics (must be implemented exactly)
- For sort=created_at_desc:
  - Primary ordering: created_at in descending order, with NULL values placed after all non-null values (i.e., NULLS LAST semantics).
  - Secondary ordering (tie-breaker): compare UUID strings converted to the standard lowercase representation and order ascending by that lowercase UUID string.
- For sort=title_asc:
  - Primary ordering: title in ascending order using Unicode code-point ordering (i.e., ordering by code point sequence). Ensure your data store or query explicitly uses code-point ordering rather than a locale/collation that changes ordering semantics; if the DB defaults to a collation that is not code-point order, use an expression or collation setting to force binary/code-point ordering.
  - Secondary ordering (tie-breaker): compare UUID strings converted to the standard lowercase representation and order ascending by that lowercase UUID string.

Notes on implementation details (store-agnostic guidance)
- Apply the ORDER BY according to the rules above before applying LIMIT/OFFSET (or your service's pagination mechanism). The server must sort the full filtered result set and then return the requested page slice.
- If the primary datastore supports NULLS LAST and case/collation control (e.g., SQL databases), implement ORDER BY created_at DESC NULLS LAST, LOWER(uuid) ASC or ORDER BY title <code-point-collation> ASC, LOWER(uuid) ASC. If it does not support NULLS LAST, implement an equivalent expression (for example, ORDER BY (created_at IS NULL) ASC, created_at DESC) that places NULLs after non-null values.
- For UUID tie-breaker: use a comparison on the canonical lowercase ASCII string of the UUID (e.g., LOWER(uuid::text) or an explicit lowercase conversion) for deterministic ordering. Do not rely on case-insensitive comparisons that are locale-dependent—explicitly normalize to ASCII lowercase for ordering.
- Do not modify filtering rules or how pagination request parameters are named/parsed; only change ordering and validation as described.

3) Output and representation
- The server must not alter stored UUID values solely for ordering. Ordering must use the lowercase representation for comparison, but returned UUID fields may keep their existing representation unless your API standard requires normalization. If you choose to normalize returned UUID strings to lowercase, document that change in the API changelog since it could be a visible change.

4) Tests / Acceptance criteria (backend)
- Unit tests for the query builder or ORM layer that assert generated ORDER BY expressions for both sort values, including explicit NULL placement for created_at_desc and the LOWER(uuid) tie-breaker.
- Integration tests that exercise end-to-end responses:
  - Default behavior when sort omitted -> results equivalent to sort=created_at_desc.
  - created_at_desc orders by created_at descending with all records having NULL created_at after ones with non-null created_at; when created_at values tie, order by lowercase UUID ascending.
  - title_asc orders by title using Unicode code-point ordering; when titles tie, order by lowercase UUID ascending.
  - Pagination: verify that sorting is applied to the full filtered set and the returned page is the slice of that sorted set (i.e., ORDER BY then LIMIT/OFFSET). For multi-page results, the union of page results across pages in order must equal the full sorted sequence.
  - Invalid sort parameter -> HTTP 422 returned with the expected error code/shape.
- Add a deterministic end-to-end test where two records are identical in primary sort key but have different UUIDs that differ only by letter case; ensure ordering uses the lowercase-string comparison to produce a stable ordering.

5) Performance guidance
- Implement the ordering in the datastore layer (DB or index engine) rather than pulling all rows into application memory. If possible, create or adapt indexes that support the ORDER BY patterns (for example, an index on created_at (desc) plus LOWER(uuid) or an index on title (binary/code-point collation) plus LOWER(uuid)) to avoid expensive sorts on large datasets. However, index creation must follow your team's existing DB change and migration process.

6) Backwards-compatibility and coordination
- Do not change existing filtering behavior or request/response fields except for the validation behavior (422) when an unsupported sort is supplied. Coordinate any visible changes (e.g., if you decide to normalize UUID output) with clients and document them in the API changelog.

Do not invent additional sort values or change other API parameter names; implement strictly the two allowed enum values, the default, the 422 behavior for invalid values, the two specified ordering semantics (including NULLS LAST for created_at_desc and Unicode code-point ordering for title_asc), and ordering-before-pagination.
